similarly, the Tich\u00fd/Miller problem does not stop scientists from identifying the best-tested."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-inductive methodological rule grounded in the objective history of severe testing; however, accepting this defense costs us the ability to claim that such theories are 'more likely' to be true or reliable in a probabilistic sense, restricting rational action to a gamble on the theory with the highest verisimilitude (truth-likeness) despite the known logical difficulties in formally defining that metric for false theories.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If one demands that rational action requires a positive probability assignment to the success of the theory, then Popper's view collapses into irrationalism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the formal definition of verisimilitude is strictly required for any comparison of false theories, then Popper's defense fails logically.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the analogy to natural selection is interpreted as providing a normative justification rather than a descriptive parallel, the argument commits the naturalistic fallacy.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument proceeds by distinguishing between 'justification' (which requires induction) and 'preferability' (which relies on the asymmetry of falsification). It posits that choosing the best-tested theory is akin to choosing the strongest player in a tournament based on past matches, not to predict they will win the next match with high probability, but because they have survived the most rigorous attempts to eliminate them. This shifts the normative core from 'expectation of truth' to 'adherence to the critical method.' The mechanism explicitly addresses the Tich\u00fd/Miller collapse of verisimilitude by treating verisimilitude as a regulative ideal rather than a computable metric, arguing that while we cannot calculate it, the process of severe testing is the only known engine for approaching it.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
